simple: a short name for a node's path.
analogy: "the main office" instead of "building 2, floor 1, room 7".
precise: a property of /aliases whose value is a full path; /chosen/stdout-path may name an alias, optionally followed by ":" and options such as "115200n8".
source: D1 of F4-27 (devicetree.org, "Devicetree Specification": /aliases, /chosen stdout-path, ranges, #address-cells) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of a kernel that is written again for every CPU family.
analogy: the notes about one particular building.
precise: the files that use CPU-specific instructions, registers or calling conventions (entry code, exception vectors, page-table format, interrupt-controller and timer drivers, the firmware interface), behind interfaces that the arch-neutral core calls.
source: D2 of F4-23 (This project's Systems Curriculum, section 9 (Track D: 9.1 the checklist table, 9.5 milestones D1–D7 with their acceptance tests) and section 10.2 (architecture-neutrality checklist).) — the project's own page, opened in this build

simple: kernel code that compiles and behaves the same on every CPU.
analogy: the timetable rules, which mention no room numbers.
precise: code with no inline assembly, no fixed page or cache-line size, explicit byte order for external data, atomics only through the language's atomic types, and no assumption about pointer width beyond what it states (curriculum 10.2).
source: D2 of F4-23 (This project's Systems Curriculum, section 9 (Track D: 9.1 the checklist table, 9.5 milestones D1–D7 with their acceptance tests) and section 10.2 (architecture-neutrality checklist).) — the project's own page, opened in this build

simple: 64 bytes at the start of a kernel file that tell a loader how to place it.
analogy: the label on a parcel: which way up, how heavy, where to put it.
precise: a branch instruction, a second code word, text_offset, image_size, flags, reserved words and the magic "ARM\x64" at offset 56, as described by the Linux arm64 booting document.
source: D4 of F4-24 (The Linux kernel documentation, "Booting AArch64 Linux" (Image header, CPU state at entry, x0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an instruction that stops the CPU from letting some accesses overtake others.
analogy: "post everything above before anything below".
precise: dmb orders memory accesses before it against those after it, for a given domain (ish: inner shareable, osh: outer shareable, sy: full system) and type (ld, st, or both); dsb additionally waits until they complete; acquire loads (ldar) and release stores (stlr) order one access.
source: D2 of F4-26 (Arm, "Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture": memory model, barriers (DMB, DSB), acquire/release instructions, MPIDR_EL1, TPIDR_EL1, cache maintenance) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the number the UART divides its clock by to get the bit rate.
analogy: how many ticks of the school clock make one beat of the drum.
precise: divisor = UARTCLK / (16 × baud) as a fixed-point number: integer part in IBRD, 6-bit fraction in FBRD; 48 MHz and 115200 give 26.042 → IBRD 26, FBRD 3.
source: D4 of F4-27 (Arm, "PrimeCell UART (PL011) Technical Reference Manual" (IBRD, FBRD, LCR_H, CR, FR)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the chain of programs that run before your kernel on a Pi.
analogy: the building's own caretaker who opens up, reads the instructions pinned to the door and lets you in.
precise: on the Pi 3 and 4 the VideoCore GPU's boot ROM starts first (from the SoC on the Pi 3, via an EEPROM bootloader on the Pi 4), loads the firmware from the SD card's FAT partition, which reads config.txt, loads the devicetree and kernel8.img, and releases the Arm cores.
source: D3 of F4-27 (Raspberry Pi Ltd, Raspberry Pi documentation: "The config.txt file", boot flow, the GPIO header and UART configuration) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: devicetree addresses can be written in a bus's own numbering; ranges says how to turn them into the CPU's addresses.
analogy: room numbers in the original architect's numbering, with a conversion table at the start of each wing.
precise: a node's reg is in its parent bus's address space; the parent's ranges = <child-base parent-base size> triples map it upwards; an empty ranges means identical, a missing one means not translatable.
source: D1 of F4-27 (devicetree.org, "Devicetree Specification": /aliases, /chosen stdout-path, ranges, #address-cells) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one 32-bit number inside a devicetree property.
analogy: one box on a form, always the same size.
precise: a big-endian 32-bit unit; a 64-bit address is two cells, and the parent node's #address-cells and #size-cells say how many cells each entry of a child's reg property uses.
source: D1 of F4-23 (devicetree.org, "Devicetree Specification" (curriculum D1 and D5 reading), chapters on the devicetree structure, standard properties (compatible, reg, #address-cells, #size-cells, phandle, /chosen) and "Flattened Devicetree (DTB) Format") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: "I am taking this interrupt" and "I have finished with it".
analogy: lifting the receiver, and hanging it up.
precise: a read of the context's claim register (claim) and a write of the same source ID to it (complete); until completion, the PLIC does not forward that source again.
source: D1 of F4-29 (RISC-V International, "RISC-V Platform-Level Interrupt Controller Specification") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of names a device answers to, most specific first.
analogy: the language a visitor speaks, written on the visitor's badge, so the school can call the right interpreter.
precise: a string list such as "arm,pl011", "arm,primecell"; a driver binds to a node whose list contains a string it knows.
source: D1 of F4-23 (devicetree.org, "Devicetree Specification" (curriculum D1 and D5 reading), chapters on the devicetree structure, standard properties (compatible, reg, #address-cells, #size-cells, phandle, /chosen) and "Flattened Devicetree (DTB) Format") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: small library functions the compiler calls for operations the CPU cannot do in one instruction.
analogy: a calculator the rulebook assumes every building owns.
precise: for example __udivdi3 (64-bit unsigned division on 32-bit CPUs), __aeabi_uldivmod (the Arm EABI equivalent), __atomic_fetch_add_8 (64-bit atomics without hardware support) and AArch64's outline-atomics helpers; normally supplied by libgcc or compiler-rt and libatomic, which freestanding kernels must link or replace.
source: D4 of F4-30 (GCC "libgcc" and LLVM "compiler-rt" documentation (integer and atomic helper routines); Arm, "Run-time ABI for the Arm Architecture" (__aeabi_uldivmod); GCC AArch64 options (-moutline-atomics)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how wide int, long and pointers are.
analogy: the size of the standard paper in each building.
precise: LP64 (64-bit Linux and BSD on x86-64, AArch64, RISC-V 64, LoongArch 64, s390x, ...): int 32, long and pointers 64 bits. ILP32 (32-bit CPUs): int, long and pointers 32 bits; long long is 64 on both.
source: D2 of F4-30 (ISO/IEC 14882 (C++) and ISO/IEC 9899 (C): integer literal types, variadic arguments; GCC and clang documentation of the format attribute) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a data structure that firmware hands to the kernel, describing the machine's hardware as a tree of named nodes with properties.
analogy: the plan of the building that the caretaker leaves on the principal's desk (a mapping proposed for the registry in this course's notes).
precise: the format defined by the Devicetree Specification; in memory it is a flattened devicetree blob (DTB) whose address the boot protocol passes in a register.
source: D1 of F4-23 (devicetree.org, "Devicetree Specification" (curriculum D1 and D5 reading), chapters on the devicetree structure, standard properties (compatible, reg, #address-cells, #size-cells, phandle, /chosen) and "Flattened Devicetree (DTB) Format") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the binary form of a devicetree.
analogy: the plan folded into an envelope, with a table of contents on the front.
precise: a header (magic 0xd00dfeed, total size, offsets of the blocks, version), a memory-reservation block, a structure block of 32-bit big-endian tokens (BEGIN_NODE, END_NODE, PROP, NOP, END) and a strings block of property names.
source: D1 of F4-23 (devicetree.org, "Devicetree Specification" (curriculum D1 and D5 reading), chapters on the devicetree structure, standard properties (compatible, reg, #address-cells, #size-cells, phandle, /chosen) and "Flattened Devicetree (DTB) Format") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: which byte of a multi-byte number is stored first.
analogy: writing a date day-first or year-first.
precise: little-endian stores the least significant byte at the lowest address (x86, Arm and RISC-V as normally used, LoongArch); big-endian the most significant (s390x, MIPS and PowerPC in the configurations tested here). Data with a defined byte order (devicetree: big-endian; virtio: little-endian) must be read with explicit conversions.
source: D3 of F4-30 (Cohen, D., "On Holy Wars and a Plea for Peace" (the origin of the terms big- and little-endian), and the virtio specification's statement that modern devices use little-endian fields) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the register that says why an exception happened.
analogy: the note the doorbell system writes: who rang and why.
precise: ESR_EL1: exception class in bits 31:26, instruction length in bit 25, an instruction-specific syndrome in bits 24:0; for aborts the low six bits are a fault status code. FAR_EL1 holds the faulting address and ELR_EL1 the return address.
source: D1 of F4-24 (Arm, "Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture" (curriculum D1 reading): the AArch64 exception model (exception levels, vector tables, ELR/SPSR/ESR/FAR), the ESR_EL1 description (exception classes, fault status codes), HCR_EL2, CNTHCTL_EL2, SPSR) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: AArch64's privilege levels, numbered 0 to 3; a higher number has more control.
analogy: the floors of the building: pupils, principal, the real principal above, the caretaker's office.
precise: EL0 runs applications, EL1 an operating-system kernel, EL2 a hypervisor, EL3 the secure monitor (firmware); exceptions are taken to the same or a higher level, and eret returns to the same or a lower one.
source: D1 of F4-24 (Arm, "Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture" (curriculum D1 reading): the AArch64 exception model (exception levels, vector tables, ELR/SPSR/ESR/FAR), the ESR_EL1 description (exception classes, fault status codes), HCR_EL2, CNTHCTL_EL2, SPSR) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the architecture's built-in clock and per-CPU alarms.
analogy: the master clock and each teacher's alarm.
precise: a system counter read through CNTPCT_EL0 at the frequency in CNTFRQ_EL0, plus per-CPU timers such as the EL1 physical timer (CNTP_TVAL_EL0, CNTP_CTL_EL0) whose interrupt is a PPI.
source: D1 of F4-25 (Arm, "Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture" (curriculum D2 reading): the VMSAv8-64 translation system (descriptors, TCR, MAIR, TTBR, SCTLR), memory attributes, barriers and TLB maintenance, the generic timer (CNTFRQ, CNTPCT, CNTP_TVAL, CNTP_CTL)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: Arm's standard interrupt controller.
analogy: the doorbell panel: front desk, desks outside each teacher's room, a hatch in each wall.
precise: in GICv3, a distributor for shared interrupts, one redistributor per CPU for its private interrupts, and a CPU interface reached through ICC_* system registers; interrupt IDs 0–15 are SGIs, 16–31 PPIs, 32 and up SPIs.
source: D2 of F4-25 (Arm, "Arm Generic Interrupt Controller Architecture Specification, GIC architecture version 3 and version 4" (distributor, redistributors, CPU interface system registers, interrupt types)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: RISC-V's word for a hardware thread: one thing that runs instructions.
analogy: one teacher.
precise: a hardware thread with its own registers and program counter; a core may hold several; harts are numbered by hart ID (mhartid, readable only in M-mode, so firmware passes it in a0).
source: D1 of F4-28 (RISC-V International, "The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume II: Privileged Architecture" (privilege modes, S-mode CSRs, Sv39, PMP)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an interrupt that fires again as soon as it is handled, forever.
analogy: the alarm that rings again because nobody set the next time.
precise: a level-triggered source whose condition is never cleared: the controller signals it again immediately after end-of-interrupt, and the CPU does nothing else.
source: D2 of F4-25 (Arm, "Arm Generic Interrupt Controller Architecture Specification, GIC architecture version 3 and version 4" (distributor, redistributors, CPU interface system registers, interrupt types)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a devicetree list that says which interrupt controller and line each output goes to.
analogy: the wiring chart from the panel's outputs to each teacher's room.
precise: pairs of (phandle of a hart's riscv,cpu-intc node, cause number); on the PLIC node, the n-th pair describes context n: cause 11 means M-mode external, 9 S-mode external.
source: D3 of F4-29 (The Linux kernel's devicetree bindings for the RISC-V PLIC (sifive,plic-1.0.0, riscv,plic0), riscv,cpu-intc and RISC-V cpus (mmu-type, riscv,isa)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an interrupt one hart sends to another.
analogy: a note under another teacher's door.
precise: SBI send_ipi(hart_mask, hart_mask_base) raises a supervisor software interrupt (cause 1) on each hart in the mask; the receiver clears sip.SSIP.
source: D2 of F4-29 (RISC-V International, "RISC-V Supervisor Binary Interface Specification" (TIME, IPI, HSM, SRST; error codes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a register holding up to eight kinds of memory, which descriptors refer to by number.
analogy: a legend on the locker map: colour 0 means "fragile, handle in order", colour 1 means "ordinary shelf".
precise: MAIR_EL1 has eight 8-bit attribute fields; a descriptor's AttrIndx (bits 4:2) selects one; this kernel uses 0x00 (Device-nGnRnE) at index 0 and 0xff (Normal, write-back cacheable) at index 1.
source: D1 of F4-25 (Arm, "Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture" (curriculum D2 reading): the VMSAv8-64 translation system (descriptors, TCR, MAIR, TTBR, SCTLR), memory attributes, barriers and TLB maintenance, the generic timer (CNTFRQ, CNTPCT, CNTP_TVAL, CNTP_CTL)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the rules for the order in which other observers see one CPU's memory accesses.
analogy: notes sent by internal post: on one school's post every note arrives in the order written; on another, notes to different rooms may overtake each other.
precise: x86-64 is total store order (stores are seen in program order; only a later load may pass an earlier store); AArch64 and RISC-V are weakly ordered (accesses to different addresses may be observed in any order unless a barrier, acquire or release orders them).
source: D2 of F4-26 (Arm, "Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture": memory model, barriers (DMB, DSB), acquire/release instructions, MPIDR_EL1, TPIDR_EL1, cache maintenance) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: each CPU's own address, as a set of up to four numbers.
analogy: building, floor, corridor, room.
precise: MPIDR_EL1's Aff3–Aff0 fields; the devicetree's cpu nodes give each CPU's affinity value in reg, and PSCI and the GIC use it to name a CPU.
source: D2 of F4-26 (Arm, "Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture": memory model, barriers (DMB, DSB), acquire/release instructions, MPIDR_EL1, TPIDR_EL1, cache maintenance) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the usual open-source firmware that implements SBI.
analogy: the caretaker who stays in the building.
precise: M-mode firmware that initialises the platform, protects its own memory with PMP, and jumps to the next stage in S-mode with a0 = hart ID and a1 = devicetree address; QEMU's riscv64 virt loads a bundled copy by default.
source: D3 of F4-28 (OpenSBI project documentation (firmware types, boot flow, domains)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a compiler option that turns atomic operations into calls to helper functions.
analogy: sending every delicate job to a specialist instead of doing it in the room.
precise: GCC's default for AArch64 Linux targets: each atomic becomes a call to a __aarch64_* helper that picks LSE instructions or exclusive load/store pairs at run time; a freestanding kernel has no such helpers and builds with -mno-outline-atomics.
source: D9 of F4-24 (GCC manual, AArch64 options (-mgeneral-regs-only, -mstrict-align, -moutline-atomics)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: atomic operations compiled as calls to helpers that choose the best instruction at run time.
analogy: asking the building's office how to do a job, instead of doing it the one way you know.
precise: with -moutline-atomics (a default for some AArch64 Linux targets), the compiler emits calls such as __aarch64_ldadd8_relax that test for the LSE atomic instructions; a kernel disables it with -mno-outline-atomics or provides the helpers.
source: D4 of F4-30 (GCC "libgcc" and LLVM "compiler-rt" documentation (integer and atomic helper routines); Arm, "Run-time ABI for the Arm Architecture" (__aeabi_uldivmod); GCC AArch64 options (-moutline-atomics)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: variables of which every CPU has its own copy.
analogy: each teacher's own register book on their own desk.
precise: a structure per CPU, found through a register only that CPU sees: TPIDR_EL1 on AArch64 (like GS base on x86-64, tp or sscratch on RISC-V).
source: D2 of F4-26 (Arm, "Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture": memory model, barriers (DMB, DSB), acquire/release instructions, MPIDR_EL1, TPIDR_EL1, cache maintenance) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a number that one devicetree node uses to point at another.
analogy: a room number written on a note in another room.
precise: a 32-bit value in a node's phandle property; properties such as interrupt-parent and interrupts-extended refer to nodes by it.
source: D1 of F4-23 (devicetree.org, "Devicetree Specification" (curriculum D1 and D5 reading), chapters on the devicetree structure, standard properties (compatible, reg, #address-cells, #size-cells, phandle, /chosen) and "Flattened Devicetree (DTB) Format") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: everything around the CPU that a kernel has to know about: memory, devices, firmware, how the other cores start.
analogy: the school building, as opposed to the principal's rules.
precise: in this course, the answers to the nine rows of the curriculum's checklist (CPU manual, firmware handoff, memory map, interrupt controller, timer, console, storage, SMP start-up, other devices) for one machine.
source: D2 of F4-23 (This project's Systems Curriculum, section 9 (Track D: 9.1 the checklist table, 9.5 milestones D1–D7 with their acceptance tests) and section 10.2 (architecture-neutrality checklist).) — the project's own page, opened in this build

simple: RISC-V's standard controller for device interrupts.
analogy: the doorbell panel with a light per door and a "taken" register per teacher.
precise: per-source priority registers, per-context enable bits and priority threshold, and a per-context claim/complete register; reading claim returns the highest-priority pending source and marks it in service; writing its number back completes it. A context is one hart in one privilege mode.
source: D1 of F4-29 (RISC-V International, "RISC-V Platform-Level Interrupt Controller Specification") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: RISC-V's three levels of permission: machine, supervisor, user.
analogy: the caretaker's level, the principal's level, the classrooms.
precise: M-mode (firmware; always present, full access, controls physical memory protection), S-mode (the OS kernel; virtual memory), U-mode (applications); each has its own trap registers (mcause, scause, ...).
source: D1 of F4-28 (RISC-V International, "The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume II: Privileged Architecture" (privilege modes, S-mode CSRs, Sv39, PMP)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a standard set of firmware calls for switching CPUs and the whole machine on and off.
analogy: the forms sent up to the caretaker's office.
precise: the Arm Power State Coordination Interface: function IDs such as PSCI_VERSION, CPU_ON, SYSTEM_OFF, invoked with hvc or smc under the SMC Calling Convention; the devicetree's /psci node names the instruction.
source: D6 of F4-24 (Arm, "Arm Power State Coordination Interface (PSCI)" specification (function IDs, PSCI_VERSION, SYSTEM_OFF)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a firmware call that switches on another CPU and starts it at an address you give.
analogy: asking the caretaker to unlock another classroom and send a teacher to a given page of the plan.
precise: PSCI function 0xC4000003 (64-bit), arguments target MPIDR affinity, entry point address, context ID; the target starts at the entry point with the MMU and caches off and the context ID in x0.
source: D1 of F4-26 (Arm, "Arm Power State Coordination Interface Platform Design Document" (DEN0022): CPU_ON, AFFINITY_INFO, SYSTEM_OFF, return codes, entry state) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: QEMU running one Linux program for a foreign CPU on your machine.
analogy: a visiting teacher from another building, translated sentence by sentence.
precise: user-mode emulation: QEMU translates the program's instructions and turns its Linux system calls into the host's; no kernel, devices or privileged instructions are emulated.
source: D5 of F4-30 (QEMU documentation: user-mode emulation (qemu-user) and its -strace option) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a board arrangement in which a bad kernel can always be undone.
analogy: keeping the old key until the new lock works.
precise: a dedicated SD card for experiments, a known-good card kept aside, the kernel swapped as one file, a serial console that works before the kernel does, and a power switch within reach.
source: D3 of F4-27 (Raspberry Pi Ltd, Raspberry Pi documentation: "The config.txt file", boot flow, the GPIO header and UART configuration) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the calls an S-mode kernel makes into M-mode firmware.
analogy: the service hatch in the caretaker's office.
precise: an ecall from S-mode with the extension ID in a7, the function ID in a6 and arguments in a0–a5; the firmware returns an error in a0 and a value in a1; extensions include TIME, IPI, RFENCE, HSM (hart state), SRST (system reset) and DBCN (debug console).
source: D2 of F4-28 (RISC-V International, "RISC-V Supervisor Binary Interface Specification" (version 1.0 or later: base, TIME, IPI, RFENCE, HSM, SRST, DBCN, legacy extensions)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: SBI calls to start, stop and query harts.
analogy: asking the caretaker to wake another teacher.
precise: hart_start(hartid, start_addr, opaque) starts a stopped hart in S-mode at start_addr with a0 = hart ID, a1 = opaque and translation off; hart_status returns 0 (started), 1 (stopped) or a transition state.
source: D2 of F4-29 (RISC-V International, "RISC-V Supervisor Binary Interface Specification" (TIME, IPI, HSM, SRST; error codes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two ways to set a timer alarm from S-mode: ask the firmware, or write a CSR directly.
analogy: asking the caretaker to set the alarm, or having your own alarm clock.
precise: SBI set_timer(stime_value) programs the next timer interrupt and clears the pending one; the Sstc extension adds the stimecmp CSR so S-mode can do this without an ecall. The time CSR counts at the devicetree's timebase-frequency.
source: D2 of F4-29 (RISC-V International, "RISC-V Supervisor Binary Interface Specification" (TIME, IPI, HSM, SRST; error codes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the three kinds of ordinary GIC interrupt: from software, private to one CPU, shared.
analogy: a note one teacher slips under another's door; a teacher's own alarm; the front door's bell.
precise: software-generated interrupts (IDs 0–15, sent by writing ICC_SGI1R_EL1), private peripheral interrupts (16–31, one copy per CPU, such as the timer), shared peripheral interrupts (32–1019, routed to a CPU by the distributor).
source: D2 of F4-25 (Arm, "Arm Generic Interrupt Controller Architecture Specification, GIC architecture version 3 and version 4" (distributor, redistributors, CPU interface system registers, interrupt types)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a way to start the other cores: they wait, watching a memory location, until the kernel writes an address there.
analogy: each waiting teacher watches a mailbox; when a page number appears, they go.
precise: devicetree enable-method = "spin-table" with a cpu-release-addr per CPU; the core waits with wfe, reads the 64-bit slot, and branches to it when it becomes non-zero; the kernel writes the entry, cleans the line to memory, and sends sev.
source: D2 of F4-27 (The Linux kernel's "Booting AArch64 Linux" document (Documentation/arch/arm64/booting.rst) and its cpu-enable-method bindings (spin-table)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: RISC-V's three-level page tables for 39-bit virtual addresses.
analogy: the locker map, in RISC-V's handwriting.
precise: satp.MODE = 8 selects it; three levels of 512 eight-byte entries; an entry with any of R, W, X set is a leaf (4 KiB, 2 MiB or 1 GiB); the physical page number is in bits 53:10.
source: D1 of F4-28 (RISC-V International, "The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume II: Privileged Architecture" (privilege modes, S-mode CSRs, Sv39, PMP)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a named CPU control or status register, read with mrs and written with msr.
analogy: a switch or a dial on the wall of a staff room.
precise: registers such as SCTLR_EL1, VBAR_EL1, ESR_EL1, whose suffix names the lowest exception level allowed to access them.
source: D1 of F4-24 (Arm, "Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture" (curriculum D1 reading): the AArch64 exception model (exception levels, vector tables, ELR/SPSR/ESR/FAR), the ESR_EL1 description (exception classes, fault status codes), HCR_EL2, CNTHCTL_EL2, SPSR) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the tables the MMU reads to turn a virtual address into a physical one.
analogy: the map of lockers: locker number to real cupboard.
precise: in VMSAv8-64 with a 4 KiB granule, tables of 512 eight-byte descriptors; each level resolves 9 bits of the address; a descriptor is invalid, a table pointer, a block (1 GiB at level 1, 2 MiB at level 2) or a page (4 KiB at level 3).
source: D1 of F4-25 (Arm, "Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture" (curriculum D2 reading): the VMSAv8-64 translation system (descriptors, TCR, MAIR, TTBR, SCTLR), memory attributes, barriers and TLB maintenance, the generic timer (CNTFRQ, CNTPCT, CNTP_TVAL, CNTP_CTL)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the registers that say where traps go and what happened.
analogy: the doorbell's report card.
precise: stvec (handler address and mode), scause (bit 63 = interrupt; low bits = cause code), sepc (the instruction that trapped), stval (faulting address or instruction bits), sstatus (interrupt enable, previous mode); return with sret.
source: D1 of F4-28 (RISC-V International, "The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume II: Privileged Architecture" (privilege modes, S-mode CSRs, Sv39, PMP)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the block of code the CPU jumps into when an exception happens.
analogy: a row of sixteen doorbells, one per kind of caller and situation.
precise: 16 entries of 0x80 bytes at the address in VBAR_ELx, which must be 2 KiB aligned: four groups (current EL with SP_EL0, current EL with SP_ELx, lower EL in AArch64, lower EL in AArch32), each with synchronous, IRQ, FIQ and SError entries.
source: D1 of F4-24 (Arm, "Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture" (curriculum D1 reading): the AArch64 exception model (exception levels, vector tables, ELR/SPSR/ESR/FAR), the ESR_EL1 description (exception classes, fault status codes), HCR_EL2, CNTHCTL_EL2, SPSR) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: virtio devices found at fixed memory addresses instead of on a PCI bus.
analogy: the same delivery truck, parked at a numbered bay instead of booked through the bus office.
precise: a virtio transport with a register block per device (magic "virt", version, device ID, features, queue addresses, notify, status); version 2 is the modern transport, version 1 the legacy one; the devicetree lists each slot with compatible virtio,mmio.
source: D3 of F4-26 (OASIS, "Virtual I/O Device (VIRTIO) Version 1.x", sections on the split virtqueue, virtio-blk and "Virtio Over MMIO") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: no memory may be both writable and executable.
analogy: a locker is either for notes you may change, or for the instructions you follow, never both.
precise: a mapping policy: code pages read-only and executable, data pages writable and execute-never (PXN/UXN), read-only data neither writable nor executable.
source: D1 of F4-25 (Arm, "Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture" (curriculum D2 reading): the VMSAv8-64 translation system (descriptors, TCR, MAIR, TTBR, SCTLR), memory attributes, barriers and TLB maintenance, the generic timer (CNTFRQ, CNTPCT, CNTP_TVAL, CNTP_CTL)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
